title: wrestling all night, limping, renamed
carry: you'll limp and you'll be blessed
tomorrow: "we will do and we will hear"

lines: A MAN WRESTLES HIM TILL DAWN.
cards: It's the night before the hardest meeting of his life. Twenty years ago Jacob cheated his twin brother Esau out of their father's blessing and ran. Now he's coming home, and Esau is on the road with four hundred men.
Jacob sends his family across a river called the Jabbok and stays behind, alone, in the dark. And then, the text says, a man wrestles with him until the break of dawn. No name.
No warning. No explanation. Just two bodies in the dirt all night long.
Today: the wrestler, and the name the whole people still carries.

teach.h: YAAKOV — THE ONE WHO GRABS THE HEEL.
teach.b: Jacob. In Hebrew, Yaakov, from the word for heel, because he was born holding on to his twin brother's heel. He's been grabbing ever since.
Who is he fighting? The text calls him a man.

teach.h: A MAN, AN ANGEL, OR GOD?
teach.b: The prophet Hosea calls him an angel. Jacob himself names the place Peniel, the face of God, because he says he saw God face to face. One old midrash says it was Esau's angel.
The Torah doesn't settle it, and maybe that's the point: some nights you can't tell who you're fighting. As dawn comes, the stranger can't win, so he touches Jacob's hip and wrenches it.
And Jacob, hurt, still won't let go: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." The blessing is a new name.
"Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel; for thou hast striven with God and with men, and hast prevailed."
Israel: one who wrestles with God. A whole people named not for someone who obeyed quietly, or never doubted, but for someone who fought all night and held on. And he doesn't walk away clean.

teach.h: I WILL NOT LET THEE GO, EXCEPT THOU BLESS ME.
teach.b: The sun rises, and Jacob is limping. The Torah says that's why the children of Israel don't eat the sinew of the thigh, and observant Jews still don't. A food law that remembers an injury.
He's hurt, and he's renamed, in the same morning.

how: Jews read Jacob's wrestling in the Torah portion Vayishlach each year; the name Israel, the people's name, comes from this story, and observant Jews still do not eat the sciatic nerve of an animal because of Jacob's hip.

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: not eaten, to remember the limp

s: the Torah says clearly who Jacob wrestled
the text says a man; Hosea says an angel; Jacob says he saw God. it doesn't settle it.
Jacob refuses to let go until he's blessed
"I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."
his hip is wrenched, and he limps into the sunrise.

games.q: you're Jacob. it's dawn, your hip is wrenched, and the stranger says: let me go. what do you do?
o: hold on until he blesses you.
ask him to heal your hip.
games.why: he holds on: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." the blessing is a new name, Israel.

practice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Think of one thing you're wrestling with right now: a decision, a person, a question. Don't try to win it in the next minute.
Just hold on to it, the way Jacob held on, and ask what blessing might be in it. If you pray, you can ask for that blessing.

wordCard.voice: Jacob. The heel-grabber who wrestled until dawn, came away limping, and was renamed Israel. Ninth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Jacob, linked in the story to akev, heel.
